parties:
Modina Vegetable & Oil Refinery Industries (Private) Ltd ------ Appellant
Vs.
M.T. Dolares and others ------Respondents.
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J.:- This appeal by the Plaintiff-appellant is from the judgment and order dated 12-8-93, passed by the learned Admiralty Judge of the High Court Division, in Admiralty Suit No. 21 of 1993, returning the Plaint on the ground that the suit is not maintainable and that there is no cause of action for the suit. 

 2. The suit was filed for a money Decree for Tk. 10,50,23,103.70 for non-delivery of cargo valued at Tk. 7,15,53,049.00 and damages amounting to Tk. 3,34,70,054.70. Upon filing of the suit, the Plaintiff-appellant filed an application for arrest of the vassel M.T. Dolares, Defendant-Respondent No. 1 then berthed at Chittagong Port, and the Court passed an order of arrest of the vessel and show cause. A joint written objection was filed by Defendant-respondents Nos. 1-5, namely, the vessel, its owner and parties interested, the Master of the vessel, the commercial managers of the owner of the vessel and the local agent of the vessel. The appellant subsequently filed an application for an order of ad-interim injunction for restraining the local agent of the vessel, Respondent No. 5, from selling, shifting or in any way disposing of the cargo of 4,108.23 M.T. of crude degummed Soyabean oil stored in the Jamuna Oil Company Ltd., Storage Tank Terminal, Chittagong. The impugned order of returning the Plaint was passed in the interlocutory proceeding. The vessel M.T. Dolores was released from arrest, but no order was passed on the application for ad-interim injunction. 

 3. The Plaintiff-appellant alleged in the Plaint that it entered into a contract for supply of 4,108.23 M.T. of crude degummed soyabean oil from any South American Port to Chittagong and opened a Letter of Credit in favour of the supplier, Devon Industries Ltd. of Singapore and that its Banker Janata Bank (defendant No. 11) carried on the transaction. The supplier (Devon) had entered into a Voyage Charter party with the owner of the said vessel M.T. Dolores through Defendant No. 4, Commercial Manager of the owner, acting through Defendant No. 7 Ocean Wide Freight Brokers Pte., Singapore, which issued the bills of lading in respect of the Plaintiff's cargo. The Commercial Manager of the owner of the vessel, Defendant No. 4, by a Telex dated 23-6-93 to the local agent of the vessel, Defendant No. 5, confirmed that the bills of lading of the Plaintiff were in order. The Plaintiff was informed of the arrival of the vessel M.T. Dolores at Chittagong Port by Defendant No. 5 which requested the Plaintiff to nominate the tank terminal in which it intended to store its cargo which the Plaintiff directly informed Defendant No. 4. After the arrival of the vessel in Chittagong Port, the Plaintiff and other consignees of Chittagong bound Soyabean oil carried out quantification survey and the Plaintiff's cargo of 4,084.775 M.T. was stored at the Jamuna Oil Company Ltd. (defendant No. 6) Storage Tank Terminal, Chittagong, as nominated by the Plaintiff. The Plaintiff, thereafter, requested Defendant No. 5 to issue a delivery order to enable the Plaintiff to take delivery from the tank terminal its cargo whereupon Defendant No. 5 sent a telex massage to the Plaintiff stating that they have been instructed by the owners/carriers not to issue any delivery order for the entire cargo of 9,500 M/tons CDSO discharged into customs bonded tanks at Chittagong until/unless the original bills of lading as issued at load ports are surrendered by charterers/suppliers (Devon) to the owners. Hence the suit. 

 4. In their Written objection to the arrest of the vessel, Defendants Nos. 1-5 stated that the suit was not maintainable at the instance of the Plaintiff under the Admiralty jurisdiction, that the Plaintiff had no cause of action, that the Plaintiff had no title in the goods and was neither the owner nor the consignee nor the assignee of the bills of lading and that the Plaintiff had no locus, standi to file the suit. They stated that it was beyond their knowledge that the Plaintiff had any contract for supply of Soyabean oil with the supplier Devon Industries Sd. Bhd of Singapore, nor are they aware of the Letter of Credit. They claimed that they did not sign any charter party agreement and they did not authorise Ocean Wide Freight Brokers Pte. Ltd., Singapore, to issue any bill of lading in respect of the suit consignment. They had already discharged the cargo meant for delivery at Chittagong port into Chittagong bonded tanks and it is the responsibility of the Plaintiff to take delivery of their cargo on production of the original bills of lading issued at the load Ports by the. Master or by the owners or owner's managers or any authorised local agent thereof or on production of a letter of indemnity executed by any scheduled bank covering the value of the alleged cargo. It is because of the failure of the Plaintiff or its agent to submit such bills of lading that delivery order could not be issued. 

 5. At the hearing of the interlocutory matter before the lamed Admiralty Judge, a number of documents were filed by both sides. Upon consideration of the plaint, written objection, the documents aforesaid and submissions, the learned Admiralty Judge held that as the Plaintiff had failed to produce the "original" bills of lading, it can neither claim to be the owner nor the consignee nor the assignee of any bill of lading of any goods. The learned Admiralty Judge also found that the original bills of lading, which the plaintiff has, lies with the Janata Bank and in the absence of retirement of the bills of lading from the Bank, the Plaintiff is not entitled to delivery order. The learned Admiralty Judge also noticed photocopies of several bills of lading filed by the Ship—owner-respondents and other correspondence and found that several other parties arc claiming to be in possession of the "original" bills of lading in respect of the suit consignment. The Plaintiff is, therefore, not en-titled to the delivery order and there is no breach of contract giving rise to any cause of action for the suit. 

 6. Leave was granted to consider the appellant's submissions that facts, as stated in the plaint, and the limits imposed by law upon the Admiralty Court, must be sufficient for the conclusion whether a suit would be tried in the Admiralty Court. The learned Admiralty Judge acted without jurisdiction, it was submitted, in travelling beyond the plaint and the law in returning the plaint. It failed to notice that Defendant No. 5 refused to make any delivery order not because the Plaintiff had not returned the original bills of lading from Janata Rank, but because it was holding the bills of lading issued by Defendant No. 7, Ocean Wide Freight Brokers Pte. Ltd,. Singapore. The Plaintiff's case that the Commercial Managers of the owner of the vessel defendant No. 4 had acted through Defendant No. 7 which had entered into a voyage charter party with the owner of the vessel, and that the bills of lading issued by Defendant No. 7 were stated to be in order by Defendant No. 4 in its telex massage dated 23-6-93 to Defendant No. 5 were not taken into consideration by the learned Admiralty Judge. It was submitted that non-issuance of the delivery order was a breach of contract which brings the suit squarely within the ambit of Section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. 

 7. During the hearing of the appeal, Dr. Kamal Hossain, learned Counsel for the appellant, confined his arguments to the points on which leave was granted. He referred to Halsbury's Laws of England, 4th Edition, volume 339 at para 505, Carver's Carriage by Sea, 12th Edition, Volume 1, page 40 at para 50 and Carrige of Goods by Sea, 13th Edition, Volume 2, page 1135 at para 1624 in support of his submission that a bill of lading may be issued not only by the owner of the ship but also by its agents. In the present case, he submits, his entire cse is based on the fact that the bills of lading, which the plaintiff produced, have been issued by the authorised agents of the ship-owner and, therefore, the bills of lading need not be issued at the load Port. 

 8. Mr. M. Hafizullah, learned Counsel for Respondents Nos. 2-3, on the other hand, reiterated his submissions made before the High Court Division, lamely, that the suit was not maintainable before the Admiralty Court because the Plaint did not disclose any cause of action to attract the jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court under Section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. He submits that several other parties produced copies of original bills of lading to the master of the ship in respect of the suit consignment. These bills of lading were issued at load ports showing Devon Industries of Singapore as the notifying party with whom the ship-owner contracted to deliver the goods. Unless the bills of lading issued at load port showing Devon as the notifying party are surrendered by the Plaintiff, the master of the vessel is not obliged to give delivery of the consignment to the Plaintiff. He submits that the learned Admiralty Judge rightly decided the question in full accord with the provisions of Section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. The Plaintiff, in the absence of the original bill of lading, is neither the owner nor the consignee nor the assignee of any bill of lading of any goods. It has no cause of action for the suit and there is no breach of contract so as to attract the mischief of Section 6. 

 10. Be that as it may be, this Court held in Saleh Steel Industries case (supra) that in the absence of a power to reject the plaint, the Admiralty Court can return the plaint to the Plaintiff for presentation to a Court with proper jurisdiction if there is no cause of action triable by it or in case it otherwise lacks jurisdiction. 

 13. As far as the plaintiff is concerned, his prima facie cause of action is his statements in the plaint regarding his invoice, the bills of lading, the charter party agreement entered into by Devon Industries of Singapore, the authority given to Defendant No. 7 through Defendant No. 4 to issue the bills of lading, the acceptance of the bills of lading by Defendant No. 4 in its telex message to Defendant No. 5, the import manifest, the quantification survey made by the Plaintiff and the unloading of the cargo at the nominated tanker of the Plaintiff. 

 14. The Respondents joined issue with the Plaintiff contending that they did not sign any charter party agreement, that they did not authorise Defendant No. 7 to issue any bill of lading in respect of the suit consignment and that some other parties have submitted to them what they consider to be the "original" bills of lading. 

 15. Therefore, what is the "original" bill of lading in this case will depend upon the truth or otherwise of the respective cases of the parties. At this stage, the learned Admiralty Judge could not have jumped to the conclusion that what the ship-owners were insisting to be the "original" bills of lading are the real "original" bills of lading in this case. The Plaintiff, in its plaint, did not refer to those bills of lading claimed to be "original" by the ship-owners. The Admiralty Court does not know yet what are the Plaintiff's objections to the "original" bills of lading produced by the ship owners. It is much too premature to dismiss the Plaintiffs bills of lading and clothe the ship-owners' "original" bills of lading with a stamp of approval. Before coming to a final decision, the learned Admiralty Judge should have waited till the evidence was complete. He could not have finally decided that the Plaintiff was not the owner, assignee or consignee of the bills of lading of the suit consignment, that there was no breach of contract and that there was no cause of action for the suit. 

 16. The Respondents did not refuse to give a delivery order, because the Plaintiff had not retired the bills of lading from the Janata Bank, but because, the bills of lading held in original by the Janata Bank are themselves not acceptable to them, not being issued in the load port and Devon of Singapore not being a notifying party therein. If at all the bills of lading of the Plaintiff are held to be valid, the Plaintiff will have to retire them and produce the same in original before the ship-owner or its agents prior to getting a delivery order in its favour.
